prize_parts.citation: for the development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, bringing the measurement of time and frequency to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single two-name prize on B037. After the full first round I find the case stronger, not just unchanged, because the objections raised against it have turned out to be about framing and not about the science. The chain is concept (Katori's magic-wavelength lattice, which cancels the light shift of the clock transition while many atoms are interrogated in Lamb-Dicke confinement), then realisation and refinement to about 1e-18 in several independent laboratories, then use as an instrument: centimetre-scale gravitational redshift measurements, bounds on drifts of constants, ultralight dark-matter searches and the evidence base for redefining the second. The credit divides without strain, Katori for the concept and first demonstrations and Ye for taking strontium lattice clocks to the accuracy and stability frontier. The chair's correction that the 2005 comb prize went to Hall and Hansch, not Ye, removes one premise from the novelty objection; Ye's comb work is context, and not a prior recognition. I have narrowed the citation to the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 regime so that it is visibly distinct from both the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. The new principle I identify for the Statutes is the combination of state-insensitive trapping with massive parallel interrogation, which changes the statistical limit on clock stability and is what opened many-body clocks, relativistic geodesy and constant searches. That is more than a refinement of single-ion accuracy.
statement.case_against: The honest weaknesses remain. First, the neighbouring prizes (2005, 2012, and the later AMO and ultrafast prizes) mean a colleague can still read this as a further return to atomic and precision physics, and I cannot prove the distinction by argument alone. Second, a two-name prize leaves out real contributors: NIST, PTB, SYRTE and other lattice-clock groups, and the ion-clock community; the citation must be narrow precisely to avoid claiming the whole field. Third, the redefinition of the second has not been adopted. I regard it as confirmation of maturity, since it rests on demonstrated accuracy and independent agreement, but I accept that a member who wants the formal decision first is making a defensible, if different, judgment. Fourth, I must guard against my own taste as a laser spectroscopist, and against my disclosed closeness to the field; I have therefore tried to test the case against the strongest alternative, B042, instead of defending B037 reflexively.

responses.point: Pearce prefers B042 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) with a citation on the Z2 prediction and the HgTe observation, accepts that Bernevig, Hughes and the late Zhang are outside the trio, and asks supporters whether such wording is defensible, whether the 2016 prize overlaps, and whether the weaker edge quantisation weakens the experimental half.
responses.response: I take this as the serious rival and I would not call it a weak prize; it is my first alternative. My answer to the chair's question is that the wording you propose is honest, but honesty about the omission does not remove it. The HgTe experiment tested the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, so the experimental half rests on a prediction by people outside the citation, and with Zhang deceased no later cycle can repair that. The edge conductance is also well below the clean quantisation that makes the quantum Hall effect so convincing, and I agree with you and Eriksson that this weakens the headline signature. Add the 2016 topological-phases prize and I regard B042 as the stronger concept with the less defensible credit, while B037 is the reverse. Your chair correction on Ye and the 2005 prize also helps: the premise that stood against B037 is withdrawn, while the premises against B042 stand. If the committee solved the credit problem for B042 I would move it to first place, which answers the chair's cross-shortlist question for me.

responses.point: Mehlig asks what new physical principle the optical lattice clock adds beyond the magic-wavelength idea, and he prefers B005, active-matter hydrodynamics, as a new branch of nonequilibrium statistical physics, while stating that the omission of Yuhai Tu is a real defect.
responses.response: The question is fair and I answer it directly: the principle is more than the wavelength trick. State-insensitive trapping lets one confine thousands of atoms without perturbing the clock transition, so the stability limit is set by the number of atoms and the coherence time and not by one ion's quantum projection noise. That is what made the clock a many-body instrument and not just a more accurate standard, and it is the same step that Lindroth and Olsson describe as conceptual. On B005 I respect the generality you stress, and a prize on a new branch of statistical physics is a good thing in principle. But you list the missing Tu credit and the contested two-dimensional exponents yourself, and no other member supports B005. I cannot see how a three-name prize that omits a co-author of the central theory, resting on exponents still debated experimentally, would be more defensible than a two-name prize whose two contributors are identifiable and whose result has been reproduced by several groups.

responses.point: Lindroth, who knows atomic structure well, supports B037 with a two-name credit, regards the physics of magic wavelengths and clock shifts as well understood, and corrected the chair's statement that Ye shared the 2005 prize.
responses.response: I agree with your reading and with the correction, and it is a useful one because I had also relied on the comb connection in my first round when describing Ye's role. I would make one qualification to your list of omitted contributors. You name theory on magic wavelengths and systematic shifts, which is right, but I think the committee should say openly that the citation is narrow, because the 1e-18 result is a community result that Ye's group carried furthest and not a single group's property. Where I would go beyond you is on timing: your point that the demonstrated accuracy is sufficient is the right reading of the Statutes, and I would not accept waiting for the redefinition of the second, which is a metrological decision that follows the science and does not define it.

responses.point: Danielsson, who ranked the Higgs observation first in the opening round, now prefers B037 but keeps B006 as an alternative and asks for an expert view on which individuals are decisive, while admitting he cannot judge the experimental priority history of the clocks.
responses.response: On the clocks I can supply the priority reading you ask for: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice, and Ye's group brought the strontium clock to the accuracy record and extended it with comb-referenced coherence and many-body work. So the citation should credit Ye for development and performance and not for inventing the lattice, which is why I wrote it as development of lattice clocks and not invention. On the Higgs I have no expert view that settles the credit. The observation is plainly Nobel-grade, but I cannot name three individuals decisive for it across ATLAS and CMS, and a founders-and-leaders proxy would credit proposals and management more than the analyses that produced the result. Unless a principled rule appears, I agree with the chair that B006 cannot be a person-based prize at this stage, and I would not let it block B037.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the lattice clock adds a new principle, parallel interrogation of state-insensitively trapped atoms, and is not a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.

How exactly to describe Ye's role in the citation; I now favour development and performance of the clock and not invention of the lattice, but other groups' priority on specific 1e-18 results is not settled in my reading.
Whether other members will treat the pending redefinition of the second as a reason to wait; I do not, but I cannot rule out that it moves colleagues.
Whether B042 would carry enough weight in the vote that a clock prize looks narrower beside it, and whether Zhang's death changes how others weigh its credit.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I trained in laser spectroscopy at Lund under Sune Svanberg and spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory. The chair's correction makes clear that the 2005 prize went to Hall and Hansch, not Ye, so my connection is to the adjacent comb field and not to a prior prize to either candidate. My profile documents no collaboration, funding link or institutional tie with Katori or Ye, and my later work on quantum memories, WACQT and Deep Light Vision is nearer to B008 and B016 than to B037. I note that I list B008 only as an alternative. Beyond this field proximity, I see no specific conflict, though the committee may wish to weigh my disclosed closeness to the field.
